headline: Inlet blues crash the night shift as bay water hits 68 degrees
subhead: Outgoing tides after midnight are producing doormat fluke and slot bass in crystal-clear water.
body_markdown:
The night bite is absolutely on fire right now. Water temps hit 68 degrees in the bay this week — a solid 4-degree jump from the ocean side of the inlet — and that thermal gradient is stacking bait on every flood tide and holding predators on the ebb. I've been working the inlet from 11 PM to 3 AM, and it's been lights-out fishing.

The bluefish showed up in force Sunday night. Big choppers, 8 to 12 pounds, crashing bait in the rip on the outgoing. I'm throwing 5-inch Yozuri Mag Darters on 50-pound fluoro — you need the heavy leader or these blues will cut you off in seconds. The flat head on the Mag Darter gives it subtle action even in the strong current, and that D-wood drag is deadly when the water's moving. Pop-pop-pause retrieve, let the current work the bait on the drift.

What's really interesting is how clean this water is. Crystal clear, almost tropical-looking blue-green that you don't usually see until August. The stripers are visible 10 feet down, and they're spooky as hell. When the blues are blitzing on top, I'm swinging a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white Zoom fork tail underneath the school. That's where the bass are — just under the chaos, picking off wounded bait.

Fluke fishing in the bay has been exceptional. The Ponquogue Bridge area is holding some real doormat potential. I'm drifting 30 feet of water with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working the drop-offs where the channel cuts close to the bridge pilings. Outgoing water is key — that's when the current pushes bait off the flats and concentrates it in the deeper cuts. Had a 6-pounder Tuesday night that hit right at the tide change.

The weakfish are starting to show at the bridge too. Nothing huge yet, but 14 to 16-inch fish on the incoming tide after dark. Small Deadly Dicks and 1/4-ounce bucktails with pink teasers are getting bit. The fish are holding in 15 to 20 feet, right where the current breaks around the bridge structure.

Bait situation is solid. Peanut bunker are thick in the bay, especially around the canal entrance. Spearing are showing up in good numbers near the inlet mouth. If you're fishing bait, a simple fishfinder rig with fresh bunker chunks is producing both bass and blues. Fish it tight to the inlet jetties on the outgoing — that's where the current creates the ambush points.

One thing I'm watching closely is how the new moon spring tides are affecting the bite. We're getting big water movement, especially on the outgoing, and that's flushing a lot of bait out of the back bay areas. The inlet becomes a funnel, and everything has to pass through that narrow opening. Position yourself on the ocean side of the inlet around midnight, and you'll intercept fish following the bait.

The only downside has been boat traffic during the day. Big boats running through the inlet are scattering the schools, so the night bite has been much more consistent. Less pressure, better fishing.

Looking ahead, we've got a full moon Friday, which means even bigger tides. I'm expecting the inlet to really drain hard at sunset, and that should trigger the first serious run of weakfish we've seen this season. The bay-to-ocean temperature differential should hold for another week, so this pattern isn't going anywhere soon. Get out there after dark — the fish are feeding.
